title: Jack Kilby and the Circuit That Fit on a Sliver of Germanium
summary: When Jack Kilby switched on an oscillator at Texas Instruments in September 1958, a sliver of germanium produced a steady electrical signal. Its fine gold wires tell another part of the story. They made the demonstration work, but each connection still had to be made by hand. Kilby’s route from a Kansas ice storm to that Dallas laboratory helps explain why he thought an entire circuit could be built from semiconductor material. Robert Noyce, Jean Hoerni and a team at Fairchild found a way to put the wiring into the manufacturing process itself. This biography follows those distinct achievements into a calculator that printed its answers on paper and, decades later, into the processors that run neural networks. Across those devices a practical question keeps returning. How far must an electrical signal travel to do useful work?

title: Reports of AI-related child sexual abuse material rise 8,400% in two years, data shows
summary: Calls for governments to recognise sexual exploitation of children as preventable public health emergency Reports of artificial intelligence being used to sexually exploit children have risen by more than 8,400% in two years, research has found. A report by the Edinburgh-based Childlight – Global Child Safety Institute says AI-related child abuse material, including deepfakes using “nudify apps”, had risen from about 4,700 in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025. title: UK exposed to polycrisis of threats amid government ‘complacency’
summary: Lords report calls for urgent new approach to resilience planning in face of cyber-attacks, sabotage and climate crisis Ministers are complacent in the face of fast-changing and increasingly interconnected threats to the UK, and must act quickly to increase national resilience to possibly very major crises, a parliamentary report has found. While Labour recently launched a “Be Ready” campaign, advising households to have stocks of food and water, most of the public are unaware of the scale of potential threats from cyber-attacks, proxy acts of violence or strikes on underseas cables, as well as natural disasters such as extreme weather and flooding, it said.
